extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/metaphysics (interested in philosophy of religion and foundational scientific concepts)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical philosophical analysis of 'ultimate' religious and scientific concepts (e.g., God/Absolute, First Cause, Space, Time, divisibility of matter), focusing on conceivability, internal coherence, and conceptual representability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceivability as the test of acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is not a question of probability, or credibility, but of conceivability.” — hypotheses must be representable in thought; if the elements of a hypothesis cannot be put together in consciousness, they are unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory theory must be conceivable as an actual thought; mere verbal intelligibility is insufficient. If an idea can only be entertained by abstaining from trying to render it into actual thought (i.e., as a pseud-idea), it fails this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject assumptions of self-existence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Self-existence is rigorously inconceivable”; any hypothesis that ultimately relies on the assumption of self-existence (nakedly or under disguise) is vicious and unthinkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this to atheistic, pantheistic, and theistic accounts alike: if the account invokes any entity as self-existent to terminate a regress, this move is conceptually illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid explanations that entail infinite regress
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation by an external agency commits us to an infinite series of such agencies and therefore does not solve the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explanatory account that merely pushes the question back (introducing an endless chain of causes) is unsatisfactory; theories should not rely on endless causal series as a resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Cause must be conceived as infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument: it is impossible to consider the First Cause as finite, since a finite First Cause implies something outside it that would be uncaused, undermining causation; hence the First Cause must be infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If positing a First Cause, consistency requires ascribing infinitude rather than finitude—recognize, however, that this leads to other conceptual problems discussed elsewhere (e.g., inconceivability).

rubrics_metrics.name: First Cause must be independent/absolute (no dependence or internal necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The First Cause must be independent; if dependent it cannot be first; it also must have no internal necessities or relations which would imply a higher cause. Thus it must be 'absolute' — total, perfect, including all power and transcending all law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attributing to the First Cause any internal determining principles or necessary relations; such attributes would imply a higher cause and contradict its status as First Cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes ascribed must be mutually coherent (no internal contradictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes commonly ascribed to an absolute being (e.g., Infinite Power vs Infinite Goodness; Infinite Justice vs Infinite Mercy; Infinite Wisdom vs Infinite Freedom) may be mutually contradictory and therefore incoherent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a theistic or metaphysical account, test whether the set of divine/absolute attributes can coexist without contradiction; incompatible pairs invalidate the purported explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Absolute cannot coherently contain relations or internal plurality
rubrics_metrics.description: The Absolute, as conceived, is incapable of necessary relations to anything else or of containing an essential relation within itself (e.g., being composed of parts, attributes, or subject-object of consciousness). If it did, the relative would be primary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ascribe to the Absolute any internal multiplicity, part-relations, or subject-object structure; such ascriptions either dissolve the absoluteness or result in contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanations must account for transition from Absolute/Infinite to Relative/Finite without contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Absolute becomes a cause (i.e., the source of the relative/finite), one must explain how activity/causation (which implies relation/volition/consciousness) can arise without destroying the attributes of absoluteness or infinitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A credible metaphysical account should coherently explain how the relative can arise from the absolute (or show that it cannot) rather than merely asserting the transition; 'escape' by temporal succession or distinctions that reintroduce contradictions is inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pseud-ideas / symbolic conceptions of the illegitimate kind
rubrics_metrics.description: Many ultimate hypotheses (atheistic, pantheistic, theistic) involve symbolic or pseudo-conceptions (e.g., 'a square fluid' or 'moral substance') that cannot be rendered into actual thoughts and so are illegitimate elements of theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag and reject elements of theories that function only as symbolic placeholders without conceptual content; a sound account should minimize reliance on such pseudo-ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptual representability requirement for scientific concepts (Space and Time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Space and Time cannot be coherently treated as non-entities, attributes of entities, or as ordinary entities with attributes; yet we are compelled to think of them as existing. Their conception often degenerates into pseud-ideas (incomprehensible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scientific concepts must be assignable attributes and representable in thought; if a conception (e.g., Space as an entity, or Kantian forms as subjective conditions) is either self-contradictory or cannot be thought of without circularity, it should be regarded as conceptually problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kantian solution (Space/Time as forms of intellect) fails the conceivability test
rubrics_metrics.description: If Space and Time are forms of the intellect (conditions of consciousness), they cannot at the same time be objects of consciousness; thus Kant's proposition, though verbally intelligible, cannot be rendered into an actual idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid accepting solutions that make the conditions of thought also the objects of thought in a way that renders the theory incoherent; require conceptual clarity on whether a notion is condition or content of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about ultimate scientific dichotomies (e.g., infinite divisibility vs fundamental parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The debate whether matter is infinitely divisible or composed of indivisible ultimate parts presents two alternatives that are each unrepresentable in thought (infinite process requires infinite time; indivisible ultimate parts carry paradoxes about surfaces and further division).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat absolute and ultimate scientific dichotomies with skepticism if neither alternative can be satisfactorily conceived; theories should avoid committing to final metaphysical extremes that are impossible to represent mentally.
